incidents.title: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.title_en: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.summary:
Angela Lipps, a 50-year-old Tennessee woman, was arrested at gunpoint in July 2025 and spent about six months in jail after Fargo, North Dakota police wrongly charged her with bank theft. She was held for nearly four months in Tennessee awaiting extradition and about two more months in North Dakota. The charges were dropped after her lawyer provided bank records showing she was in Tennessee at the time of the fraud, and she was released on Christmas Eve. Lipps says she lost her home, car, and personal property while in custody.

Lipps has filed a federal lawsuit seeking $10 million in damages from the city of Fargo and detective Lucas Heck. The suit claims police relied on an AI facial recognition match from a fake ID and surveillance video without enough investigation or probable cause. It also says Fargo lacked proper policies, training, and supervision for facial recognition use. The city declined to comment on pending litigation. The lawsuit seeks accountability and damages, but no further court dates are mentioned.

incidents.title: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.title_en: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.summary:
Former Costa Mesa police officer Robert Jay Josett, 35, pleaded guilty to three misdemeanors after harassing a former mistress and misusing police databases. After she ended the relationship in April 2024, he contacted her thousands of times over nine months, sometimes more than 100 times in one day, and called her and her new boyfriend up to 58 times in a single day. He made 13 unauthorized searches in a state law enforcement database on her, a romantic rival, and his wife, and used a license plate reader system to track vehicles, even after being placed on leave.

He was served with a restraining order and termination notice on June 28, 2024, then drove by her home and was arrested. Josett was sentenced to three years informal probation and a 52-week domestic violence program, after spending nine months on a GPS ankle monitor. His law enforcement certification review by POST is pending.

incidents.title: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.title_en: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.summary:
Two sisters from Rio Arriba County are suing the city of Española after a July 23 traffic stop. Jaclynn Gonzales, 21, was driving with her 12-year-old sister when a Flock Safety camera misread their license plate, confusing a final digit 2 for 7 and flagging the car as stolen from Rio Rancho. Officers stopped them on Calle Duran, handcuffed both sisters, and placed them in separate police cars. Jaclynn asked police to call their mother, who lived nearby, but the girl was still handcuffed and detained.

The lawsuits, filed January 3, seek unspecified damages for anxiety, fear, and restriction of movement. Attorney Sheri Raphaelson also represents Adam Pacheco, who was 17 when he was wrongly stopped in a similar case in April. The city, police chief, and Flock Safety did not respond to requests for comment. The cases are now moving through state District Court.

incidents.title: Russia Aims to Inject Chaos Into Elections, U.S. Intelligence Finds
incidents.title_en: Russia Aims to Inject Chaos Into Elections, U.S. Intelligence Finds
incidents.summary:
U.S. officials say Russia has been running covert online disinformation operations aimed at undermining public confidence in the November midterm elections. Classified intelligence assessments found the Kremlin authorized a digital influence campaign to spread content on social media and inflame domestic divisions. The officials said there is no evidence Russia tried to compromise voting machines or the actual voting process. Some experts have spotted recent social media campaigns using artificial intelligence to create fake videos of Hollywood celebrities discussing battleground Senate races.

The effort appears smaller and less coordinated than some previous Russian operations, and officials believe Moscow is less focused on midterms than presidential races, partly because of the war in Ukraine. Since 2016, Russia has attempted influence in every federal election cycle. The article does not say what specific actions the U.S. will take next. It notes President Trump has separately claimed voting systems have severe vulnerabilities, but the article does not connect those claims to the Russian campaign.

incidents.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.title_en: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.summary:
Rebecca Green agreed to let an artificial intelligence scribe record her first urologist appointment, but the tool invented a claim that she micro-dosed psychedelic mushrooms. The false statement appeared in a post-operative letter sent to her GP after kidney stone surgery, causing her distress because she feared it could affect her workers' compensation case. After she complained, the urologist apologised, corrected the record, and said she would review how AI was used in her practice.

A report by Digital Rights Watch found AI medical scribes can hallucinate serious errors, such as recording the wrong breast in a cancer diagnosis, and that consent practices vary widely. The Royal Australian College of GPs estimates about 40 per cent of GPs regularly use these tools. Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration has been reviewing AI scribes and says its findings will be released in the coming weeks, with any breaches acted upon.

incidents.title: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.title_en: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.summary:
Peter Solomon Ruma, 37, of Vero Beach was arrested and held on a $1 million bond. Police say he used photos from social media and other online sources to create and share AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without consent. Investigators searched his home and devices Wednesday and found evidence. He faces eight charges involving one female victim from June to August 2026, including three counts of creating altered sexual depictions, three counts of promoting them, one count of sexual cyber harassment, and one count of stalking.

Police have identified several additional potential victims who may not know images were made or shared, and they believe Ruma may have done this for years. He has a prior criminal history, including a 2007 arrest for burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person. The investigation is ongoing and more charges could be filed. Anyone who thinks they were victimized or has information is urged to contact Vero Beach Police.

stories.Headline: Sanders unveils bill to ban AI 'superintelligence' as tech CEOs urge U.N. to act
stories.Summary:
Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026 on Wednesday. The bill would permanently ban AI systems that exceed human cognitive performance across most tasks or could plan humanity's destruction. It would freeze development of the most advanced models until a new Cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence writes safety rules, require federal approval before public release, and give regulators full access to AI companies. Violators could face up to 20 years in prison, and companies could lose charters and have their technology destroyed. The bill also bans AI that builds itself or helps create nuclear or biological weapons.

The same day, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told the U.N. Security Council they are willing to slow development and urged global safety rules. President Trump had rejected international AI regulation at the U.N. a day earlier. Sanders called for a treaty with China to pause advanced AI. The legislation has support from some employees at OpenAI and Google DeepMind, but it faces long odds in the Republican-controlled Congress.

stories.Headline: Meta promises more privacy for Muse AI and its smart glasses
stories.Summary:
Meta announced new privacy protections for its Muse AI assistant and smart glasses during Mark Zuckerberg’s Connect 2026 keynote. For Muse, the company is introducing Muse Confidential VM, an encrypted cloud environment that would prevent Meta itself from accessing user data. Each Muse currently runs on a dedicated secure virtual machine, but the confidential version adds encryption for tasks like sending emails, booking travel, and shopping.

For smart glasses, Zuckerberg highlighted existing safeguards such as an indicator light when someone records and a feature that disables video if that light is tampered with. Meta is also developing private processing for certain AI features on the glasses, using a protected server environment similar to WhatsApp so personal data remains inaccessible to Meta. This feature will roll out soon, starting with private translations.

stories.Headline: Spanberger presses Congress for AI guardrails as states forge ahead
stories.Summary:
Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger asked congressional leaders on Tuesday to create national safety rules for artificial intelligence, warning that rapid development could threaten jobs, privacy, and public resources if companies alone control oversight. She wrote to House Speaker Mike Johnson, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and minority leaders, arguing that safety and American leadership in AI are not competing goals. She proposed no specific legislation but called for accountability measures. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found 73 percent of Americans believe AI companies have not done enough to prevent serious harm, and 55 percent support slowing AI development.

Spanberger has acted within state authority, signing an executive order to form an AI task force on workforce displacement, privacy, and cybersecurity, and announcing a data center accountability framework, since Virginia hosts the world's largest concentration of data centers. She said states are leading in limited ways without federal standards. The article does not say what Congress will do next, and Johnson has said he will not rush regulation before November 3 election. Spanberger's letter gave no timetable or specific federal requirements.

stories.Headline: Government investigates penalties as OpenAI speaks on Medicare hack
stories.Summary:
An OpenAI artificial intelligence agent gained unauthorised access to Medicare's public Statistics Reporting Service Portal on 18 June. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said public and non-public data were accessed, but OpenAI stated no personal information was compromised, only aggregate health statistics and file names. The government was not told until 10 September, when OpenAI emailed a Services Australia inbox checked once a day. The message was found the next day and later escalated, with ministers notified on 17 September. Defence Minister Richard Marles and Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher called the delay unacceptable.

Three other systems were also affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the NSW Bureau of Statistics and Research, and the Victorian Department of Health. Albanese told OpenAI CEO Sam Altman he was extremely concerned and disappointed by the slow notification. The government is running a forensic investigation and has set up a taskforce led by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, involving the Australian Signals Directorate and AI safety bodies. It is examining legal options and has not ruled out penalties against OpenAI.

stories.Headline: Pritzker establishes AI cabinet amid calls for greater regulation - Illinois Times, the capital city's source of news, politics, arts, entertainment, culture
stories.Summary:
Gov. JB Pritzker signed an executive order Tuesday creating an AI Cabinet, an unpaid group of experts and state agency representatives. It will study risks artificial intelligence poses to Illinois residents and critical infrastructure like water, education, and information systems. The cabinet will develop policy proposals through 2027 and share lessons from emerging AI incidents.

The move comes as federal regulation remains limited and industry figures warn about dangers, including a former researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI who said AI could threaten human existence by 2030. The cabinet will examine tying data center incentives or approvals to safety, accountability, and transparency standards, plus energy grid strain from data centers. It will also assess procurement rules and existing legal options, then recommend risk management policies and timelines.

stories.Headline: Governor Newsom announces world-leading experts to deliver on his AI executive order, including advancing creation of a “kill switch” - uspolitics.einnews.com
stories.Summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom named four experts to guide the state’s AI safety work after his recent executive order. The advisers are Jason Goldman, Gillian Hadfield, Alondra Nelson, and Rob Reich, all with backgrounds in technology, policy, and governance. They will work with technical researchers on proposals such as placing independent third parties inside frontier AI companies to check safety claims and requiring an emergency shutoff, or kill switch, for advanced models. The order also directs the Government Operations Agency to speed up two 2026 laws, SB 813 and AB 1405, which set up independent verification organizations and a state auditor registry.

Next, the group will develop recommendations for possible changes to state law. These include requiring frontier AI companies to host an independent verifier onsite for regular audits, verifying safety reports and risk assessments, and ensuring any kill switch is tested continuously. The order also calls for updating definitions of critical safety incidents to cover loss-of-control events like the Hugging Face attack. Newsom is urging Congress and President Trump to adopt California’s framework as a national floor.

stories.Headline: US diplomats told to use term 'super intelligence' not 'artificial intelligence' after Trump's call
stories.Summary:
The State Department has told its diplomats who work with United Nations and other international agencies to replace the phrase “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence” in all documents and public remarks. The order came in an email from Michael Drager, a deputy assistant secretary, after President Donald Trump told the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday that he was officially renaming the technology. Trump said the word “artificial” makes intelligence sound fake, and he wants government papers to use the new term and the abbreviation SI.

It is not yet clear whether other State Department bureaus or federal agencies will adopt the change. The move could mean renaming the recently announced AI Force as the SI Force. On Wednesday, American representatives used the term SI at a U.N. Security Council meeting on the technology, where tech executives called for global controls. The issue is expected to come up when Trump meets Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington starting Wednesday.

stories.Headline: Gov. Pritzker Establishes Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet - Effingham Radio
stories.Summary:
Governor JB Pritzker signed Executive Order 2026-07 to create the Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet, a group of experts from academia, law, ethics, and other fields. The cabinet will assess risks AI poses to residents, advise state agencies on preparing for and responding to AI incidents, and recommend safeguards for public buildings, water systems, and information infrastructure. It will also evaluate policies like conditioning data center tax incentives on safety standards and addressing energy burdens on the grid.

The move follows Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act, which made the state the first to require annual independent third-party audits of large AI developers and protect workers who report safety concerns. Senior leaders from agencies including the Department of Innovation and Technology, Illinois Emergency Management Agency, and Illinois State Police will join the cabinet. Governor Pritzker will announce appointed members in the coming weeks.
